name: enzyme
why: Automatic differentiation performed on LLVM IR is a genuinely odd and deep compiler idea worth understanding.

brief.what_it_is: Enzyme is an automatic differentiation plugin for LLVM. It takes existing code in the form of LLVM IR, which the homepage says can come from C, C++, Swift, Julia, Rust, Fortran, and TensorFlow, and produces the derivative or gradient of a chosen function. You mark the function with a call to __enzyme_autodiff. When the Enzyme pass runs, that call is replaced with the generated derivative function. The GitHub README also describes it as working on MLIR and as plugin for statically analyzable code.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage says the goal is to create gradients of existing source code without much additional work, instead of rewriting that code for machine learning. Working at the LLVM level lets one tool cover several languages and reuse LLVM's optimizer.
brief.how_it_works: Enzyme runs in four parts: an optional preprocessing phase, a new interprocedural type analysis that deduces the underlying types of memory locations, an activity analysis that determines which values can affect the derivative, and an optimization pass that generates derivative functions and replaces calls to __enzyme_autodiff. The homepage says it differentiates code after optimization rather than before, which it claims yields substantially faster derivatives than tools that differentiate before optimization.

brief.install_notes: Building from source needs an LLVM installation that CMake can find through LLVM_DIR, plus a lit path through LLVM_EXTERNAL_LIT, and Ninja. Package-manager routes are Homebrew, Spack, and Nix. The README says Julia, Rust, and Fortran bindings exist. The homepage points to a getting started guide and a getting involved guide, but I did not fetch them, so first-run and configuration steps are unverified. The README suggests joining the mailing list for questions.
brief.standout: Most AD tools differentiate source code or a high-level IR before optimization. Enzyme instead differentiates already-optimized LLVM IR, so one implementation can serve many languages and support GPU and parallel code, including OpenMP, MPI, and Julia tasks as the README lists.
brief.status: Maintained, with moderate confidence. The GitHub page shows about 3,127 commits, roughly 1.7k stars, 197 forks, and packages in Homebrew, Spack, and Nix. I could not see a last-commit or release date in the fetched text, so recent activity is unconfirmed.
brief.caveats: It only handles statically analyzable code, according to the README. Performance and speed claims come from the authors and their papers. Building from source needs a matching LLVM development setup. The homepage describes the project as LLVM-only, while the GitHub README says LLVM and MLIR. I did not confirm the license type, though the repo has a LICENSE file. The homepage's Compiler Explorer demo link had no URL in the fetched text.
quotes: The Enzyme project is a tool that takes arbitrary existing code as LLVM IR and computes the derivative (and gradient) of that function.
Enzyme is a plugin that performs automatic differentiation (AD) of statically analyzable LLVM and MLIR.
By differentiating code after optimization, Enzyme is able to create substantially faster derivatives than existing tools that differentiate programs before optimization.
